case_study_insert.main_stem: Dunsmore Forged Metals (DFM) is a public limited company in the metal-forging sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1998 by Gordon Dunsmore, it supplies forged steel components to construction-equipment makers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. DFM plans to invest $1,100,000 in a new forging press with heat-recovery equipment, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $22.00 a unit and a selling price of $38.00, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. DFM faces two problems: its scrap rate has reached 7.4% and client quality complaints have been rising steadily in recent months.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Waste and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The forge produced 15,000 castings last quarter with a scrap rate of 7.4%, down from 9.1% a year earlier, and scrap metal rework costs $41 per tonne. Client quality complaints have risen from 22 to 31 per month. Average delivery lead time to construction sites is 18 days. A survey of 180 plant managers found that 62% would pay 3% more for lower-carbon forged parts, and 55% require formal quality records. A maintenance audit shows 26 of 120 workers lack press-operation certification; on-the-job training is available internally and off-the-job accreditation costs $950 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Dunsmore Forged Metals as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing debt-service costs for leveraged firms. (2) The national minimum wage rises 6.2% from $14.00 to $14.87 per hour from April 2026. (3) Steel scrap and electricity input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, industrial inflation is 7.2%, and construction output grew 2.8%.

questions.question_text: DFM is financing its $1,100,000 forging press with a $600,000 bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for DFM of using the share issue rather than further bank borrowing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $500,000 share issue commits DFM to no interest payments and no capital repayment, unlike the $600,000 bank loan, so cash flow is protected while the company already bears fixed costs of $540,000 a year and a 7.4% scrap rate that creates $41-per-tonne rework spending. Money that would have serviced debt can instead fund the quality improvements needed to answer the 31 client complaints a month, protecting the $38.00 selling price without raising borrowing.

Point 2: Equity does not require collateral, so the $1,100,000 press and the firm's other assets are not exposed to repossession if construction demand, which grew only 2.8%, falls short of the 60,000-unit plan. As a public limited company DFM can raise capital from a wide shareholder base rather than depending on one lender, keeping the $600,000 loan facility available as a reserve for working capital or for the 18-day delivery lead time. Issuing shares therefore strengthens the balance sheet and spreads financial risk without adding fixed repayment obligations.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified, max 2.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to DFM's costs, scrap rate, finance and legal structure.

questions.question_text: DFM is promoting its new lower-carbon forged components. Consider a construction trade exhibition, advertisements in engineering trade magazines, or targeted LinkedIn campaigns aimed at plant managers. Which should DFM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Construction trade exhibition: A major exhibition lets DFM demonstrate forgings directly to the plant managers who buy them, supporting the 62% of 180 surveyed managers who would pay 3% more for lower-carbon parts and allowing engineers to answer questions about the new press and the 18-day delivery lead time. It is expensive in stand fees and staff time, however, and results depend on one event; with fixed costs of $540,000 a year and a $600,000 loan, a poor show would be a costly miss.

Engineering trade magazines: Print advertisements would spread awareness of DFM's lower-carbon range across the construction-equipment industry and reinforce the $1,100,000 investment. Yet magazines have long lead times, high insertion costs and wide waste circulation, reaching many readers who never specify forged components; for a specialised 120-staff forger the spend per genuine enquiry would be high and hard to measure.

Targeted LinkedIn campaigns: Social-media ads aimed by job title at plant managers are relatively cheap, quick and measurable, and can carry the 3% lower-carbon message and formal quality records straight to the decision-makers, including the 55% who require such records. They lack the physical proof of an exhibition and may miss older buyers, but cost per qualified contact is low.

Recommendation: DFM should choose the construction trade exhibition as the lead activity, with LinkedIn used for follow-up. High-value forged contracts are won on trust and visible quality, which a stand demonstrates better than print or online ads, and the 62% premium signal justifies the cost against $540,000 fixed costs. Magazine advertising is rejected as slow and untargeted, and LinkedIn alone is rejected as too passive to prove quality for a $1,100,000 investment; the smaller digital spend can support the exhibition rather than replace it.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the three promotional options with minimal application to DFM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two options with advantages and disadvantages in the context of DFM and some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to DFM with a justified recommendation explaining why magazine advertising and LinkedIn-only campaigns are rejected.

questions.question_text: DFM's scrap rate has reached 7.4% and client quality complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for DFM of using autocratic leadership to improve quality control.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets DFM impose one clear quality standard quickly across a hierarchical structure of 120 workers, which is valuable while the scrap rate stands at 7.4% and client quality complaints have risen from 22 to 31 a month. A single decisive instruction to stop a press when a fault appears prevents further defective castings, protecting the 15,000 castings made each quarter and reducing the $41-per-tonne rework burden without waiting for consensus.

Point 2: Firm direction also protects delivery and safety. With an 18-day lead time to construction sites, fast decisions about re-running or repairing a batch keep the 60,000-unit plan on schedule, which matters when 62% of 180 surveyed plant managers would pay a premium for reliable lower-carbon parts. Because 26 of 120 workers lack press-operation certification, close supervision reduces unsafe practice and inconsistent output, while founder Gordon Dunsmore's clear authority can enforce the formal quality records that 55% of buyers require.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified, max 2.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to DFM's scrap rate, complaints, delivery and certification.

questions.question_text: DFM must train 26 press operators to meet the new quality standards. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job accreditation at the technical college. Which should DFM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the press is specific to DFM's own forging equipment, costs no course fees and keeps the 26 operators producing, which helps protect the 15,000 castings made each quarter and the effort to cut the 7.4% scrap rate. It also avoids interrupting the 18-day delivery lead time. Its weaknesses are that instructors are production workers whose own output falls, that shortcuts can be passed on, and that no external certificate is awarded, a problem because 55% of 180 surveyed plant managers require formal quality records.

Off-the-job accreditation: The college course at $950 per employee gives structured press-operation skills and a recognised qualification for all 26 workers, costing $24,700 in total, modest against the $1,100,000 press. It directly addresses the audit finding that 26 of 120 workers lack certification and supports the 62% of buyers who would pay 3% more for better-documented, lower-carbon parts. However, it removes 26 staff from the floor, risking the 60,000-unit target and the 18-day lead time, and the generic course may need site-specific follow-up.

Decision: DFM should choose off-the-job accreditation, followed by short on-the-job refresher sessions. Formal certification answers the documented buyer requirement and the 7.4% scrap problem in a way informal coaching cannot, and $24,700 is small beside the $1,100,000 investment. On-the-job training alone is rejected because it produces no certificate for the 55% of buyers who demand records and may pass on bad habits; the short-term capacity loss can be managed by scheduling courses in rotation. With 26 staff forming a significant share of 120 workers, phased release is essential to protect the 18-day delivery lead time.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to DFM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of DFM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods applied to DFM with a justified decision covering certification, cost and disruption.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how DFM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 33,750 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $16.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 26,250 units vs 60,000 output; modelling the 3% lower-carbon premium against $540,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume for the $1,100,000 press; and unit-cost benchmarking at $31.00 to cut the 7.4% scrap rate.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $540,000 ÷ ($38.00 − $22.00) = $540,000 ÷ $16.00 = 33,750 units. Answer: break-even output is 33,750 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $38.00 − $22.00 = $16.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $16.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways DFM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 33,750-unit break-even output with actual output of 60,000 units, a margin of safety of 26,250 units, to see whether the new $1,100,000 press is justified and how far demand could fall before losses appear.
2. Contribution per unit of $16.00 lets DFM model the 3% premium that 62% of surveyed plant managers would pay for lower-carbon parts: a 3% rise on $38.00 adds about $1.14, lifting contribution to $17.14 and speeding recovery of the press cost.
3. Fixed costs of $540,000 and contribution of $16.00 set the sales volume needed to service the $600,000 loan and to judge whether the 2.8% growth in construction output is enough to absorb extra castings.
4. Average total cost ($540,000 ÷ 60,000 units + $22.00 = $31.00 a unit) can be tracked against the 7.4% scrap rate and $41-per-tonne rework cost, giving a clear target for the new press and a benchmark for the 11.3% rise in scrap and electricity prices.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii), max 4.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate DFM's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has DFM's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.63 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.95 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.97 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $220,000 inventories + $300,000 trade receivables + $80,000 cash = $600,000; 2025 current assets = $250,000 + $275,000 + $95,000 = $620,000. Short-term cover for 2024 is $600,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.50 and for 2025 is $620,000 ÷ $380,000 = 1.63. Excluding inventories, ($600,000 − $220,000) ÷ $400,000 = 0.95 in 2024 and ($620,000 − $250,000) ÷ $380,000 = 0.97 in 2025.

Evaluation: Both measures have improved. Short-term cover rose from 1.50 to 1.63 as current assets increased from $600,000 to $620,000 while current liabilities fell from $400,000 to $380,000. The acid test also improved from 0.95 to 0.97, showing slightly less reliance on selling inventory to meet debts, which matters while DFM services a $600,000 loan and a $1,100,000 press. However, both acid-test figures remain below 1, so the firm still depends partly on stock, and inventories have grown from $220,000 to $250,000; with a 7.4% scrap rate and 18-day delivery lead time, some of that stock may be slow-moving. The $500,000 share issue has also strengthened the long-term funding of the $1,100,000 press, so DFM is less dependent on short-term borrowing than a year ago.

Conclusion: DFM's financial position has improved, but only modestly. Both cover measures are higher and the balance sheet is less reliant on creditor finance, yet the acid test remains under 1 and inventories are rising, so management should reduce scrap and convert stock into cash before taking on more debt.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether DFM's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for DFM of installing heat-recovery equipment on its new forging press.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Heat-recovery equipment would reuse waste heat from the press, cutting the electricity element of the 11.3% rise in input costs and lowering the $22.00 variable cost per unit. This supports the 62% of 180 surveyed plant managers who would pay 3% more for lower-carbon forged parts, helping DFM win orders and defend the $38.00 selling price while reducing the $41-per-tonne rework burden associated with the 7.4% scrap rate.

Disadvantage: The equipment adds to the $1,100,000 capital already committed on top of a $600,000 bank loan and fixed costs of $540,000 a year, so it raises financial risk if the 2.8% growth in construction output proves weak. It also needs specialist maintenance that DFM may lack, since 26 of 120 workers are not yet press-certified; a breakdown could interrupt the 18-day delivery lead time and worsen the 31 monthly quality complaints if temperatures drift during forging. The 180 plant managers surveyed also expect documented quality, which the equipment alone cannot guarantee.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to DFM's waste data, survey and investment.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.75%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in steel scrap and electricity input costs will affect DFM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): If DFM's $600,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000), which is small against fixed costs of $540,000, and zero if the loan is fixed. The larger risk is that higher rates deter construction investment beyond the modest 2.8% output growth. DFM can reduce this by fixing the rate or repaying part of the loan from the $500,000 share issue.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.87 per hour): With a workforce of 120, many pressing and packing roles are hourly paid, so the wage bill rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can honestly be invented; the defensible comparison is with given productivity, 60,000 units ÷ 120 staff = 500 units per worker. If productivity stays at 500 units the $16.00 contribution can absorb the rise; if it falls, unit labour cost pushes up the $31.00 average total cost.

Input cost inflation (11.3% steel scrap and electricity): The $22.00 variable cost includes these inputs, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 11.3% that would add 11.3% × $22.00 = $2.49 per unit, or about $149,000 a year at 60,000 units (60,000 × $2.49). A portion can be recovered through the 3% premium that 62% of buyers would pay, but not all.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It hits every one of the 60,000 units, directly erodes the $16.00 contribution that funds the $1,100,000 press and cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate. The interest rise is small and manageable; the wage rise depends on productivity that DFM can influence. Input inflation is therefore the deepest threat.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to DFM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on DFM's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to DFM with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
